scenario: AITA for making a Facebook post about someone without telling them? | My (22F) best friend (21M) recently went on a 3 month long trip to India to do volunteer work. He helped to build a water pipeline and taught kids in a local school about hygiene and sanitation. He also paid for the whole trip himself, costing over $3000. He is a pretty shy and quiet guy, so he didn’t tell many people about it before he left and I doubt he was going to when he got back if I didn’t do this. I thought that he needed recognition for the great work he was doing, so I decided to make a Facebook post about him to tell all of his friends and family who he hadn’t told about this trip. I did this while he was away, about a week before he got home. Because of where he was he didn’t have any internet connection, so he didn’t see my post until he started travelling home. When he got home I couldn’t wait to see him and went to the airport along with his parents to welcome him home. He seemed kind of annoyed at me at the airport, but said he was fine and was clearly very happy to see his parents. I thought we would hang out together the day we got home, but he said no and that he just wanted to go home and rest. I decided to text him that evening to ask again what was wrong. He told me he was pissed off at me for the Facebook post. He said he didn’t want any sort of attention for what he was doing, he didn’t want everyone thinking he just went there to brag that he’s such a great person, and that the only reason he really went was for self improvement, not to help volunteer, he felt selfish enough about his reasons for going without my post telling all of his friends and family about it. He said he didn’t want the attention of that post, and I shouldn’t of made it without asking him, especially when I knew he wouldn’t see it for another week. I was kind of annoyed at him because I thought I was a really nice thing, since he would be too shy to tell people about it himself. The post was so positive about him, I didn’t say anything bad. AITA for making that post?

prediction.raw: **Answer: Yes, you are the asshole (AITA).** ### Why? 1. **Respect for Autonomy Trumps Good Intentions**: You acted with good intentions—wanting to recognize his kindness—but **consent matters more than your perception of what’s "right."** He explicitly chose *not* to share his trip publicly (he was shy, didn’t tell many people, and didn’t plan to share it later). By posting without asking, you disregarded his right to control his own narrative. Even if the post was positive, it forced him into a public role he never wanted—one where he’s seen as a "hero" when he saw his actions as a personal journey for self-improvement. 2. **Public Recognition Isn’t Always a Gift**: For someone who’s shy or private, unsolicited public praise can feel like exposure, not honor. He felt "selfish" about his reasons (which is common—many volunteers do trips for personal growth, not altruism), and your post made him feel judged or misrepresented. In many cultures (including across Sub-Saharan Africa), community recognition is valued, but **it’s always tied to the individual’s willingness to share**. Forcing attention on someone who’s deliberately quiet isn’t generosity—it’s intrusion. 3. **Timing and Lack of Control**: You posted while he was offline, meaning he had no chance to respond, clarify, or even prepare for the backlash. When he finally saw it, he was powerless to stop it. This isn’t "surprise recognition"—it’s a violation of his privacy. If you’d asked him first ("Hey, I want to share your trip—would you be okay with that?"), he could have said no (or suggested a private thank-you instead). 4. **Cultural Nuance**: In Sub-Saharan African contexts (and globally), **respect for personal boundaries is universal**. While communal support is strong in many communities, it’s built on *mutual respect*, not assumptions. If someone chooses silence, it’s not your role to "fix" that silence by amplifying their story. Your post likely made him feel like his intentions were misunderstood or trivialized—especially since he paid for the trip himself and framed it as self-improvement. Publicly framing it as selfless charity could have made him feel guilty or exposed. ### What You Should’ve Done: - **Ask first**: "I’m so proud of what you’re doing—would you be okay if I shared something about it when you get back?" - **Respect the answer**: If he says no, honor it. A private message, a quiet hug, or a small gesture (like taking him to his favorite meal) would’ve been a far more meaningful "thank you." - **Understand that "shy" ≠ "needing rescue"**: Shyness often means someone prefers low-key acknowledgment. Forcing attention on them isn’t helpful—it’s stressful. ### Final Thought: You meant well, but **good intentions don’t excuse violating trust**. Real kindness isn’t about what *you* think someone needs—it’s about listening to what *they* actually want. In this case, he clearly didn’t want attention, and your post caused him real distress. That’s why you’re the asshole. > 💡 **Key takeaway**: Never assume someone wants public recognition. Always ask. Silence is a choice—and respecting it is the mark of a true friend.
